item.title: Every Chatbot in Europe Must Now Say "I'm a Machine": Inside the EU's New AI Disclosure Law
item.body:
Starting August 2, a new phase of the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act has taken effect, and it changes something many internet users interact with every day without a second thought: the chatbot window, the customer service assistant, and the eerily convincing video clip shared on social media. Under the bloc's transparency rules, AI systems that interact with people, generate synthetic media, or read human emotions now have to say so, clearly and up front.

## What the Rule Actually Requires

The obligation, found in Article 50 of the AI Act, is built around a simple idea: people have a right to know when they are dealing with a machine instead of a human being. In practice, that translates into several concrete requirements for companies operating in the EU market.

- **Chatbots and virtual assistants** must disclose that a user is interacting with an AI system, unless it is already obvious from the context.
- **AI-generated or manipulated images, audio, and video** — commonly known as deepfakes — must be labeled as artificially generated or manipulated.
- **AI-generated or edited text** published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be marked as such, with some exceptions for content that has undergone human editorial review.
- **Emotion-recognition and biometric-categorization systems** must notify individuals when such technology is being used on them.

The rule applies broadly, covering not just AI developers but also the businesses that deploy these tools — meaning a retailer using a third-party chatbot, for example, carries its own disclosure responsibility, not just the company that built the underlying model.

## Why Regulators Are Pushing This Now

The transparency requirement is part of a staged rollout that began when the AI Act entered into force in 2024. Earlier phases banned a narrow set of "unacceptable risk" practices, such as social scoring, and set obligations for general-purpose AI model providers. This latest milestone extends the law's reach into everyday consumer-facing tools.

EU officials have framed the measure as a response to growing concern over synthetic media's role in misinformation, scams, and erosion of public trust online. As AI-generated content has become harder to distinguish from human-made material, regulators argue that a basic labeling requirement is a proportionate first step — not a ban on the technology, but a guardrail around its use.

## The Price of Getting It Wrong

Enforcement carries real financial weight. Companies found to violate the transparency obligations can face fines of up to €15 million, or 3% of their total global annual revenue, whichever amount is higher. For large multinational firms, that percentage-of-revenue calculation can dwarf the flat fee, making compliance a board-level concern rather than a minor legal footnote.

National market surveillance authorities in each EU member state are responsible for enforcement, working alongside the newly established EU AI Office, which coordinates oversight of general-purpose AI models across the bloc.

## Why This Matters Beyond Europe

Much like the GDPR reshaped global data privacy practices after its 2018 debut, the AI Act's disclosure rules are expected to influence how companies build products well outside EU borders. Many businesses find it simpler to apply one global standard for labeling and disclosure rather than maintaining separate versions of a product for different markets. Developers of chatbots, content-generation tools, and customer-facing AI assistants are already reviewing their interfaces to add clear AI-identification notices, watermarking for synthetic media, and consent flows for emotion-detection features.

For everyday users, the practical effect should be a small but meaningful one: a short label or notice indicating that the friendly voice on the other end of a support chat, or the polished video clip circulating online, was created or assisted by a machine. Whether that label meaningfully curbs misuse of synthetic media remains to be tested, but it marks one of the most concrete steps any major regulator has taken to draw a visible line between human and artificial communication.
